title: Memory size and allocation: sizeof, malloc, and free

spans.text:
RAM is the workbench used while a program runs: local variables usually live on the stack, while memory requested with `malloc`/`new` comes from the heap. Global and `static` variables live for the whole program. `sizeof(type)` reports a type's size in bytes; `sizeof(array)` reports the whole array only where it is still an array. Ten `uint16_t` values typically use 20 bytes, and `sizeof(array) / sizeof(array[0])` counts elements. When an array is passed to a function it becomes a pointer, so `sizeof(pointer)` there is not the array size.

`malloc(n)` requests uninitialized storage, `calloc(n, size)` requests zeroed storage, and `realloc(p, n)` changes a block's size. Check for `nullptr`; return these C-style allocations with `free(p)`. C++ `new` creates an object and pairs with `delete`. Never call `free` on a local array or an object from `new`, and never use `delete` on memory from `malloc`.

spans.title: Important note
spans.text: On small boards, fixed-size arrays and automatic lifetime are often simpler, faster, and safer. Repeated heap allocation and release can fragment memory: total free bytes may look sufficient while no single large block is available. Release each allocation exactly once with its matching function, then set the pointer to `nullptr`. Use `size_t` for sizes. An Arduino UNO has very little SRAM; on ESP32, `ESP.getFreeHeap()` and minimum-free-heap measurements help diagnose usage but do not replace a memory budget. Check `realloc` into a temporary pointer so failure does not lose the original block.
